title: One key, one order
intro: Choose a table that matches the lookup you need.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment. Fixture values describe an in-memory example, not database orders.
code:
TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_order,
         order_id TYPE i,
         amount   TYPE i,
       END OF ty_order.
DATA lt_orders TYPE HASHED TABLE OF ty_order
  WITH UNIQUE KEY order_id.
lt_orders = VALUE #( ( order_id = 7 amount = 100 )
                     ( order_id = 9 amount = 200 ) ).
DATA(ls_order) = lt_orders[ order_id = 9 ].

highlights.label: Define the lookup
highlights.explanation: The complete unique key is order_id. The hashed table is designed for this exact-key access.

highlights.label: Read order 9
highlights.explanation: The result is the row with amount 200. No manual sorting or numeric row position is needed.

outcome: Order 9 is found by its identity. A standard table with an empty key would express a different access choice.
caveat: This example guarantees the row exists. Handle missing keys in real code; a hashed key is not a range-search index.

title: Missing row: expected or an error?
intro: A lookup that may miss needs an explicit decision.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment. This example treats absence as expected and represents it as an unbound reference.
code:
TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_order,
         order_id TYPE i,
         amount   TYPE i,
       END OF ty_order.
DATA lt_orders TYPE HASHED TABLE OF ty_order
  WITH UNIQUE KEY order_id.
INSERT VALUE #( order_id = 7 amount = 100 )
  INTO TABLE lt_orders.
DATA(order_ref) = REF #( lt_orders[ order_id = 9 ]
                        OPTIONAL ).
DATA(found) = xsdbool( order_ref IS BOUND ).

highlights.label: Only order 7 exists
highlights.explanation: There is deliberately no order 9 in the table.

highlights.label: Keep absence visible
highlights.explanation: REF with OPTIONAL produces an unbound reference for the missing row. found is false.

outcome: A plain lt_orders[ order_id = 9 ] would raise CX_SY_ITAB_LINE_NOT_FOUND. This form avoids confusing a missing row with a real row containing initial values.
caveat: Use OPTIONAL only when absence is an allowed outcome. If the order is required, report or handle the missing-row error instead.

references.title: SAP: Default values for table expressions

title: A copy and a direct row change
intro: Watch which assignment actually changes the table.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment. Both reads succeed because fixture row 1 exists.
code:
TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_order,
         amount TYPE i,
       END OF ty_order.
DATA lt_orders TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_order
  WITH EMPTY KEY.
lt_orders = VALUE #( ( amount = 100 ) ).
READ TABLE lt_orders INDEX 1 INTO DATA(ls_order).
IF sy-subrc = 0.
  ls_order-amount = 200.
ENDIF.
READ TABLE lt_orders INDEX 1
  ASSIGNING FIELD-SYMBOL(<ls_order>).
IF sy-subrc = 0.
  <ls_order>-amount = 300.
ENDIF.

highlights.label: Change the copy
highlights.explanation: INTO copies the row. Setting ls_order to 200 leaves the table amount at 100.

highlights.label: Change the actual row
highlights.explanation: ASSIGNING points to the row. The table amount becomes 300. Each sy-subrc is checked immediately after its read.

outcome: The work area ends at 200, while the table row ends at 300. A later statement must not overwrite sy-subrc before its result is checked.
caveat: Field symbols are aliases, not independent snapshots. Do not modify sorted or hashed primary key fields through them.

title: Keep an unmatched field during mapping
intro: BASE decides whether the new structure starts with existing values.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment with small local structures. Text literals are fixture data.
code:
TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_request,
         status TYPE string,
         note   TYPE string,
       END OF ty_request.
TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_change,
         note TYPE string,
       END OF ty_change.
DATA(ls_old) = VALUE ty_request(
  status = `Approved` note = `Old note` ).
DATA(ls_change) = VALUE ty_change( note = `New note` ).
DATA(ls_plain) = CORRESPONDING ty_request( ls_change ).
DATA(ls_kept) = CORRESPONDING ty_request(
  BASE ( ls_old ) ls_change ).

highlights.label: Start with approved data
highlights.explanation: The input change has a note field but no status field.

highlights.label: Build from initial values
highlights.explanation: ls_plain gets the new note and an empty status.

highlights.label: Build from the old value
highlights.explanation: ls_kept keeps Approved and receives the new note.

outcome: The same source produces different status values. BASE preserves unmatched fields; it does not mean ignore initial source values.
caveat: If the source type also contained status, that matching field would overwrite the old status even when blank. API PATCH needs explicit field-presence rules.

title: Reject lost characters at the input boundary
intro: An identifier must fit; silently cutting it changes its meaning.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment. The four-character string is intentional test input.
code:
TYPES ty_code TYPE c LENGTH 3.
DATA(input) = `ABCD`.
DATA(ordinary) = CONV ty_code( input ).
DATA rejected TYPE abap_bool.
TRY.
    DATA(lossless) = EXACT ty_code( input ).
  CATCH cx_sy_conversion_data_loss.
    rejected = abap_true.
ENDTRY.

highlights.label: Normal conversion
highlights.explanation: The target has room for three characters. Normal conversion keeps ABC.

highlights.label: Require an exact value
highlights.explanation: EXACT rejects the nonblank character loss. The catch marks this input as rejected.

outcome: The program can report invalid input instead of storing a different identifier. Technical exactness is checked before business validation.
caveat: The sample records rejection only. A real import must return a useful field-level error and also validate permitted values.

title: A local change is copied back only on success
intro: The VALUE addition changes what an escaping exception leaves in the caller.
context: Excerpts from one local class: first the public declaration, then its implementation method. Define lcx_rejected as a CX_STATIC_CHECK subclass. A caller starts amount at 10 and catches lcx_rejected.
code:
METHODS change_amount
  CHANGING VALUE(amount) TYPE i
  RAISING lcx_rejected.

METHOD change_amount.
  amount = 20.
  RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE lcx_rejected.
ENDMETHOD.

highlights.label: Declare value passing
highlights.explanation: The method works on its own amount value. Without VALUE, CHANGING defaults to reference passing.

highlights.label: Exit with an exception
highlights.explanation: The local amount becomes 20, but the method does not complete normally, so it is not copied back.

outcome: The caller keeps 10 with this VALUE signature. With reference passing, the same assignment would already have changed the caller value to 20.
caveat: This protects the plain value only. It does not undo database writes or changes to an object reached through a copied reference.

title: Do not write through yesterday's field symbol
intro: A failed dynamic lookup must not leave a usable old target.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment. The misspelled component name is intentional test input. UNASSIGN avoids depending on newer ELSE UNASSIGN syntax.
code:
DATA: BEGIN OF ls_order,
        amount TYPE i VALUE 100,
      END OF ls_order.
FIELD-SYMBOLS <amount> TYPE any.
ASSIGN COMPONENT 'AMOUNT' OF STRUCTURE ls_order
  TO <amount>.
UNASSIGN <amount>.
ASSIGN COMPONENT 'AMUONT' OF STRUCTURE ls_order
  TO <amount>.
IF sy-subrc = 0.
  <amount> = 200.
ENDIF.

highlights.label: Clear the earlier binding
highlights.explanation: The first lookup succeeds. UNASSIGN deliberately removes that old target.

highlights.label: Check the new lookup
highlights.explanation: AMUONT does not exist. sy-subrc is not zero, so the code cannot write through the old AMOUNT binding.

outcome: ls_order-amount stays 100. Checking only IS ASSIGNED without clearing the old binding could update the wrong field after a failed lookup.
caveat: The sample skips the invalid input to show the effect. A real mapper should report it or apply an explicitly documented skip rule.

references.title: SAP: Assignment failure and ELSE UNASSIGN

title: Omitted is different from zero
intro: The caller may deliberately ask for no rows.
context: Excerpts from one local class: public declaration and matching implementation. effective is a returning integer; this method only chooses a limit and does not execute a query.
code:
METHODS choose_limit
  IMPORTING requested TYPE i OPTIONAL
  RETURNING VALUE(effective) TYPE i.

METHOD choose_limit.
  CONSTANTS co_default_limit TYPE i VALUE 20.
  IF requested IS SUPPLIED.
    effective = requested.
  ELSE.
    effective = co_default_limit.
  ENDIF.
ENDMETHOD.

highlights.label: Allow omission
highlights.explanation: OPTIONAL lets the caller omit requested.

highlights.label: Test presence, not value
highlights.explanation: choose_limit( ) returns 20. choose_limit( requested = 0 ) returns 0 because the argument was supplied.

outcome: The two calls keep their different meaning. Checking IS INITIAL would incorrectly treat an explicit zero as omission.
caveat: A wrapper that always forwards requested loses omission information. Also handle zero before any query syntax where zero might mean unlimited rows; validate negative input separately.

title: A duplicate INSERT is not an update
intro: The first order value does not silently become the second.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment. This is single-row INSERT into an internal table with a unique primary key.
code:
TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_order,
         order_id TYPE i,
         amount   TYPE i,
       END OF ty_order.
DATA lt_orders TYPE HASHED TABLE OF ty_order
  WITH UNIQUE KEY order_id.
INSERT VALUE #( order_id = 7 amount = 100 )
  INTO TABLE lt_orders.
INSERT VALUE #( order_id = 7 amount = 200 )
  INTO TABLE lt_orders.
DATA(duplicate) = xsdbool( sy-subrc = 4 ).
DATA(ls_kept) = lt_orders[ order_id = 7 ].

highlights.label: Insert the first row
highlights.explanation: Order 7 gets amount 100.

highlights.label: Try the same key again
highlights.explanation: The second INSERT fails with sy-subrc 4. The existing row still contains 100; duplicate is true.

outcome: The unique key prevents two rows, but it does not choose whether conflicting import values should be rejected or replaced.
caveat: This return-code behavior describes this single-row primary-key case. Other insertion forms and secondary-key violations can raise exceptions.

title: Group rows even when they are apart
intro: Customer 1 appears twice, with customer 2 between its orders.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment. The grouped loop calculates a per-customer total in memory; inspect total during each outer-loop iteration.
code:
TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_order,
         customer TYPE i,
         amount   TYPE i,
       END OF ty_order.
DATA lt_orders TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_order
  WITH EMPTY KEY.
lt_orders = VALUE #( ( customer = 1 amount = 10 )
                     ( customer = 2 amount = 20 )
                     ( customer = 1 amount = 30 ) ).
LOOP AT lt_orders INTO DATA(ls_order)
  GROUP BY ls_order-customer INTO DATA(customer).
  DATA(total) = 0.
  LOOP AT GROUP customer INTO DATA(ls_member).
    total += ls_member-amount.
  ENDLOOP.
ENDLOOP.

highlights.label: Notice the unsorted input
highlights.explanation: The customer sequence is 1, 2, 1. Related rows are not adjacent.

highlights.label: Visit each group and its members
highlights.explanation: The outer loop runs twice. The member loop totals 40 for customer 1 and 20 for customer 2.

outcome: GROUP BY finds both customer 1 rows without a preceding SORT. This is different from relying on adjacent control-level groups.
caveat: This is ABAP memory processing. If only database totals are required, consider a supported SQL aggregation instead. Define output order separately.

title: An empty driver must not become a full read
intro: The guard is part of correctness, not just a speed trick.
context: Method-body fragment. Own fixture table zt_demo_order has key order_id and amount. lt_ids is an already-populated internal table whose row structure has order_id with the same type as the database field. lt_orders is a compatible result table.
code:
CLEAR lt_orders.
IF lt_ids IS NOT INITIAL.
  SELECT order_id, amount
    FROM zt_demo_order
    FOR ALL ENTRIES IN @lt_ids
    WHERE order_id = @lt_ids-order_id
    INTO TABLE @lt_orders.
ENDIF.

highlights.label: Handle no requested IDs
highlights.explanation: The output is empty and the database statement is skipped when lt_ids is empty.

highlights.label: Read the requested orders
highlights.explanation: For a nonempty driver, the query matches order_id against its values.

outcome: An empty request returns no orders. Without the guard, FOR ALL ENTRIES ignores its WHERE condition for an empty driver and can read all rows in scope.
caveat: FOR ALL ENTRIES removes duplicate result rows. Keep the identity columns needed by the result and compare a join using actual result and performance requirements. Fixture tables are not SAP APIs.

title: Keep an order even without an English text
intro: Put the language rule where text rows are matched.
context: Method-body fragment. Own fixture tables: zt_demo_order has unique order_id; zt_demo_text has unique (order_id, language), plus description. language is CHAR 1. No extra business authorization is shown.
code:
CONSTANTS co_english TYPE c LENGTH 1 VALUE 'E'.
SELECT o~order_id, t~description
  FROM zt_demo_order AS o
  LEFT OUTER JOIN zt_demo_text AS t
    ON t~order_id = o~order_id
   AND t~language = @co_english
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_orders).

highlights.label: Choose right-side matches
highlights.explanation: An English text matches if it exists. Its language condition belongs to ON here.

highlights.label: Keep every left-side row
highlights.explanation: An order without an English text still appears. A WHERE t~language = co_english would remove it.

outcome: Orders stay visible even without translated text. The stated unique text key also prevents several English rows from multiplying each order.
caveat: The missing description is SQL NULL before transfer. Without null indicators, its ABAP target becomes initial, so this result alone cannot distinguish missing text from a stored empty description.

title: Send totals instead of every item
intro: Filter first, sum matching rows, then keep the required groups.
context: Method-body fragment. Own fixture table zt_demo_item contains company, currency, amount and is_cancelled. amount is an exact decimal type; amounts within each currency use the same unit convention. minimum_total is deliberately zero for the example.
code:
DATA minimum_total TYPE decfloat34 VALUE 0.
SELECT company, currency, SUM( amount ) AS total
  FROM zt_demo_item
  WHERE is_cancelled = @abap_false
  GROUP BY company, currency
  HAVING SUM( amount ) > @minimum_total
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_totals).

highlights.label: Remove cancelled items
highlights.explanation: WHERE acts on individual rows before they enter the totals.

highlights.label: Keep currency groups separate
highlights.explanation: The database calculates one total per company and currency instead of sending every item.

highlights.label: Filter the totals
highlights.explanation: HAVING keeps only groups whose calculated total is positive.

outcome: The output contains summarized rows with their currencies. There is no text join here that could multiply an item before summing it.
caveat: Currency grouping prevents mixing unlike currencies; it does not perform conversion. Real authorization, numeric range, decimal handling and measured query cost still need validation.

title: Latest requires an explicit order
intro: A one-row limit does not choose what latest means.
context: Method-body fragment. Own fixture table zt_demo_order has unique numeric order_id, customer_id and changed_at timestamp. customer_id is the method input. No matching row leaves lt_latest empty.
code:
SELECT order_id, changed_at
  FROM zt_demo_order
  WHERE customer_id = @customer_id
  ORDER BY changed_at DESCENDING, order_id DESCENDING
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_latest)
  UP TO 1 ROWS.

highlights.label: Choose the relevant customer
highlights.explanation: The conditions may match many orders, so SELECT SINGLE would not express the latest one.

highlights.label: Define the winning row
highlights.explanation: Sort by newest timestamp, then by order_id to break ties, and return at most one row.

outcome: The latest timestamp wins. If two timestamps are equal, the larger order ID wins according to this explicit example rule.
caveat: The tie-breaker is a chosen business rule, not a property of SELECT SINGLE. Validate authorization and an appropriate query plan for the real source.

title: No allowed plants means no data
intro: Do not let an empty permission result become an unrestricted filter.
context: Method-body fragment. A trusted authorization helper already supplied lt_allowed_plants as positive include-EQ range rows. lt_orders is the output. Own fixture table zt_demo_order contains order_id and plant.
code:
CLEAR lt_orders.
IF lt_allowed_plants IS INITIAL.
  RETURN.
ENDIF.
SELECT order_id, plant
  FROM zt_demo_order
  WHERE plant IN @lt_allowed_plants
  INTO TABLE @lt_orders.

highlights.label: Stop when permission is empty
highlights.explanation: The method returns an empty result before running SQL.

highlights.label: Apply mandatory permission
highlights.explanation: Only a nonempty set of allowed plants reaches the query. Optional user filters must not replace this restriction.

outcome: A user with no allowed plants receives no rows. Directly using an initial range in IN would instead impose no restriction.
caveat: This is a guard, not a complete authorization implementation. The helper must return actual permitted values; test denied API access as well as UI behavior. Exclusion-only ranges require their own policy.

title: Call the rule through one interface
intro: The coordinator asks what the rule decides, without choosing its calculation.
context: Local-interface declaration followed by an excerpt inside a coordinator method. strategy is a bound reference to an implementing class, and amount is an input. Each implementation decides its own rule without committing or sending messages.
code:
INTERFACE lif_approval.
  METHODS needs_manager
    IMPORTING amount TYPE decfloat34
    RETURNING VALUE(required) TYPE abap_bool.
ENDINTERFACE.

DATA rule TYPE REF TO lif_approval.
rule = strategy.
DATA(requires_manager) = rule->needs_manager(
  amount = amount ).

highlights.label: Agree on one operation
highlights.explanation: Every strategy accepts an amount and returns whether a manager is required.

highlights.label: Use the selected implementation
highlights.explanation: The same call reaches the actual strategy object. The coordinator does not branch on country here.

outcome: Changing the rule object changes the decision logic while the coordinator call stays the same. That is Strategy through interface polymorphism.
caveat: The snippet defines the interface and call, not complete country rules. Test each implementation against the shared promises and keep workflow side effects in the coordinator.

title: Require the helper when creating the service
intro: Give the service its dependency once, then use that exact object.
context: Constructor implementation excerpt. The class declares constructor IMPORTING repository TYPE REF TO lif_repository RAISING lcx_configuration, and a private repository attribute of that interface type. lcx_configuration is an application CX_STATIC_CHECK subclass.
code:
METHOD constructor.
  IF repository IS NOT BOUND.
    RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE lcx_configuration.
  ENDIF.
  me->repository = repository.
ENDMETHOD.

highlights.label: Reject missing setup early
highlights.explanation: A typed reference can still be initial. This check prevents creating a service that fails much later.

highlights.label: Keep the supplied helper
highlights.explanation: Production supplies a real repository; tests supply a controlled implementation of the same interface.

outcome: The constructor makes the dependency visible and valid. The service no longer needs a hidden global factory lookup in each business method.
caveat: This is an application-owned class. Do not add unsupported constructor parameters to framework-created RAP handlers; delegate to a suitable service or use supported seams.

title: Configuration chooses from known rules
intro: An unknown country must not fall back to approval.
context: Factory method excerpt. get_rule imports a two-character country value through a named character type, returns rule TYPE REF TO lif_approval, and raises lcx_configuration. Both local rule classes implement lif_approval and have no required constructor parameters.
code:
METHOD get_rule.
  CONSTANTS co_poland TYPE c LENGTH 2 VALUE 'PL'.
  CONSTANTS co_germany TYPE c LENGTH 2 VALUE 'DE'.
  CASE country.
    WHEN co_poland.
      rule = NEW lcl_polish_rule( ).
    WHEN co_germany.
      rule = NEW lcl_german_rule( ).
    WHEN OTHERS.
      RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE lcx_configuration.
  ENDCASE.
ENDMETHOD.

highlights.label: Map supported choices
highlights.explanation: The factory creates one of two known implementations of the same interface.

highlights.label: Fail unsupported setup
highlights.explanation: Blank or unknown configuration produces an error instead of silently picking a permissive rule.

outcome: Test PL, DE and an unknown value separately from the approval calculations. This is a simple factory; it is not automatically the formal Factory Method pattern.
caveat: Class and exception names are local teaching fixtures, not SAP APIs. Real configuration may also need a policy version and an audit record of the chosen rule.

title: Translate one interface into another
intro: The caller uses business-friendly fields; the adapter handles the old format.
context: Implementation of lif_payment~post. Its inputs are amount TYPE decfloat34 and a three-character currency value declared through a named character type; returning result is TYPE i. Bound legacy has execute IMPORTING ls_request TYPE ty_legacy_request RETURNING VALUE(result) TYPE i. ty_legacy_request has gross_value and curr_key matching those inputs.
code:
METHOD lif_payment~post.
  DATA(ls_request) = VALUE ty_legacy_request(
    gross_value = amount
    curr_key = currency ).
  result = legacy->execute( ls_request = ls_request ).
ENDMETHOD.

highlights.label: Translate the request
highlights.explanation: The public amount and currency become the names expected by the legacy dependency. An explicit zero is copied too.

highlights.label: Delegate one operation
highlights.explanation: The adapter calls the dependency and returns its result. The application caller need not know gross_value or curr_key.

outcome: This illustrates Adapter field mapping. A Facade would separately coordinate a larger prepare/check/post sequence.
caveat: legacy is a local illustrative interface, not a named SAP API. Real wrappers must also translate errors and preserve authorization and transaction ownership; wrapping cannot remove an internal commit or release an API.

title: Add one behavior around the same call
intro: A decorator forwards the real call while adding a small behavior of its own.
context: Implementation excerpt. This class implements lif_sender with send IMPORTING payload TYPE string RETURNING VALUE(response) TYPE string. inner is a required, bound lif_sender reference supplied through its constructor. attempts is a private integer attribute initialized to zero. The class also declares METHODS get_attempts RETURNING VALUE(count) TYPE i.
code:
METHOD lif_sender~send.
  attempts += 1.
  response = inner->send( payload = payload ).
ENDMETHOD.

METHOD get_attempts.
  count = attempts.
ENDMETHOD.

highlights.label: Wrap without replacing
highlights.explanation: The decorator counts the attempt and forwards exactly once. The inner result and escaping exception are not turned into fake success.

highlights.label: Observe the added behavior
highlights.explanation: get_attempts returns count TYPE i. The counter includes failed calls because it increments before delegation.

outcome: One wrapper invocation adds one attempt. Placing this inside or outside a retry wrapper would count attempts or logical operations differently.
caveat: The counter lives only in this object. It is neither durable logging nor a retry policy. Retrying a remote write needs explicit duplicate and unknown-outcome handling.

title: Keep the original failure when translating it
intro: Unavailable data must not become a successful empty result.
context: Method excerpt. repository is a bound local interface reference whose read_price( ) returns decfloat34 and raises lcx_repository. This get_price method returns price TYPE decfloat34 and declares RAISING lcx_price_unavailable. Both exceptions are application CX_STATIC_CHECK subclasses with the inherited PREVIOUS constructor parameter.
code:
METHOD get_price.
  TRY.
      price = repository->read_price( ).
    CATCH lcx_repository INTO DATA(cause).
      RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE lcx_price_unavailable
        EXPORTING previous = cause.
  ENDTRY.
ENDMETHOD.

highlights.label: Catch the failure you understand
highlights.explanation: Only the declared repository failure is translated here. It is not a successful no-price result.

highlights.label: Preserve the cause
highlights.explanation: The business-facing exception keeps the original exception in PREVIOUS for diagnosis.

outcome: The caller receives a clear unavailable failure instead of a zero price. Support can inspect why the repository failed.
caveat: The custom exception classes and signatures are prerequisites, not delivered SAP objects. Real user-facing messages should be translatable and must not expose sensitive technical details.

title: Test the rule itself at its boundary
intro: A threshold test must call the real calculation.
context: Two method excerpts in separate class implementations. lcl_discount declares CLASS-METHODS percent IMPORTING quantity TYPE i RETURNING VALUE(result) TYPE i. The local test class declares METHODS threshold FOR TESTING. The teaching rule is 10 percent from quantity 10, otherwise zero.
code:
METHOD percent.
  result = COND #( WHEN quantity >= 10
                   THEN 10 ELSE 0 ).
ENDMETHOD.

METHOD threshold.
  cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_equals(
    act = lcl_discount=>percent( quantity = 9 )
    exp = 0 ).
  cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_equals(
    act = lcl_discount=>percent( quantity = 10 )
    exp = 10 ).
  cl_abap_unit_assert=>assert_equals(
    act = lcl_discount=>percent( quantity = 11 )
    exp = 10 ).
ENDMETHOD.

highlights.label: Keep production behavior real
highlights.explanation: The discount decision uses the actual quantity comparison. No mock replaces it.

highlights.label: Check both sides and the boundary
highlights.explanation: Quantities 9, 10 and 11 check below, exactly at and above the threshold with independently chosen expectations.

outcome: Changing >= to > would fail the quantity-10 assertion. A mocked percent result would not detect that bug.
caveat: This illustrates test source, not an executed SAP test. Add the class definitions and required ABAP Unit attributes; validate invalid-input rules separately. No coverage percentage is claimed.

title: FILTER needs an appropriate access key
intro: A standard table can keep arrival order and offer a sorted secondary key.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment. The key customer_key is explicit and matches the equality condition.
code:
TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_order,
         customer TYPE i,
         amount   TYPE i,
       END OF ty_order.
TYPES ty_orders TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_order
  WITH EMPTY KEY
  WITH NON-UNIQUE SORTED KEY customer_key
    COMPONENTS customer.
DATA(lt_orders) = VALUE ty_orders(
  ( customer = 2 amount = 10 )
  ( customer = 1 amount = 20 )
  ( customer = 2 amount = 30 ) ).
DATA(lt_selected) = FILTER #(
  lt_orders USING KEY customer_key WHERE customer = 2 ).

highlights.label: Provide the key
highlights.explanation: EMPTY KEY does not support this basic FILTER access by itself. The secondary sorted key does.

highlights.label: Choose that key explicitly
highlights.explanation: USING KEY customer_key selects both customer 2 rows, with amounts 10 and 30.

outcome: The result contains the two matching rows. A suitable secondary key enables this FILTER form on a standard table.
caveat: Keys consume memory and maintenance work. For a condition that does not fit the key rules, prefer a clear loop or FOR expression. Check syntax support on the target release.

title: Do not invent zero as the maximum
intro: An all-negative input exposes the wrong starting value.
context: Self-contained method-body fragment. The fixture has at least one row. has_maximum explicitly represents whether any result exists.
code:
TYPES ty_values TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF i
  WITH EMPTY KEY.
DATA(lt_values) = VALUE ty_values( ( -8 ) ( -3 ) ).
DATA maximum TYPE i.
DATA(has_maximum) = xsdbool( lt_values IS NOT INITIAL ).
IF has_maximum = abap_true.
  maximum = REDUCE i(
    INIT best = lt_values[ 1 ]
    FOR number IN lt_values
    NEXT best = COND #(
      WHEN number > best THEN number ELSE best ) ).
ENDIF.

highlights.label: Handle no result separately
highlights.explanation: The guard prevents reading row 1 of an empty table. has_maximum distinguishes no value from an actual zero.

highlights.label: Start with a real candidate
highlights.explanation: The accumulator starts at -8, then becomes -3. Starting at zero would incorrectly keep zero.

outcome: The maximum is -3. The syntax is concise, but the initial value and empty-input policy still determine correctness.
caveat: Test empty, single-row, all-negative and mixed data. If the caller requires a value, reject empty input instead of relying on a separate presence flag.
